681.event_title: Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit becomes the first woman to preside over the UN General Assembly
681.place: United Nations, New York, United States
681.event: Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit, daughter of the nationalist leader Motilal Nehru and sister of Jawaharlal Nehru, led India's delegation to the United Nations and served as ambassador in Moscow and Washington after independence. In 1953 the member states elected her president of the UN General Assembly, the first woman ever to hold the post. She later served as India's high commissioner in London.
681.explanation: Her career shows how a diplomat from a family long schooled in public life, with a manner that won the respect of other states, could be entrusted with her country's voice and then chosen to preside over the assembly of nations.
681.tie_back: The kural names good family standing and the conduct that rulers value as marks of an envoy, and Pandit's background and the trust placed in her by the world's governments reflect both.
681._accuracy_note: Illustrates the family-standing and esteemed-conduct qualities well, but the sources do not document the kural's first quality, a loving nature, so the fit is partial.

682.event_title: Sergei Witte secures peace at Portsmouth without an indemnity
682.event: To end the Russo-Japanese War, President Theodore Roosevelt invited Russia's chief negotiator Sergei Witte and Japan's Baron Komura Jutaro to talks that were held at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard. Under the treaty signed on 5 September 1905, Russia gave up its rights to Port Arthur and the southern half of Sakhalin Island but paid no indemnity to Japan. Witte was made a count for his efforts.
682.explanation: Witte came out of a lost war having protected the point his government cared about most, refusing any payment, while still finding terms the other side would sign.
682.tie_back: The kural asks of an envoy loyalty to his ruler, knowledge of what serves him, and words chosen so that the other side will agree, and Witte's settlement at Portsmouth shows those three working together.
682._accuracy_note: A solid example of an envoy knowing and securing his ruler's interest, though Roosevelt's mediation also shaped the outcome and Witte's personal feelings toward the Tsar are not documented here.

683.event_title: Philosopher Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan meets Stalin as India's ambassador
683.event: Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, professor of Eastern religions and ethics at Oxford and author of works on Indian philosophy, served as India's ambassador to the Soviet Union from 1949 to 1952. Before leaving Moscow he was received by Joseph Stalin, and the Indian record of the conversation shows him explaining India's parliamentary methods and independent foreign policy, correcting Stalin's doubt that Indian women had voted, and raising complaints about Soviet press coverage of India. Stalin agreed to recall the Soviet correspondent concerned.
683.explanation: A scholar sent among powerful rulers argued his country's case point by point before one of the most feared leaders of the century and came away with a concrete concession.
683.tie_back: The kural says that the one who speaks for his king before spear-bearing rulers must be the most learned among the learned, and Radhakrishnan, an Oxford professor, was exactly such an envoy before Stalin.
683._accuracy_note: A close fit: a renowned scholar acting as envoy before a formidable ruler, though the record is India's own account of the meeting.

684.event_title: Dag Hammarskjold's mission to Peking for the detained airmen
684.date: 30 December 1954 to 13 January 1955; airmen released in 1955
684.event: Asked by the UN General Assembly to seek the release of American airmen who had served under the UN Command in Korea, Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjold travelled to Peking and negotiated directly with Zhou Enlai, since the People's Republic of China was not represented at the United Nations. Hammarskjold, who held a doctorate in economics and had been the outstanding student of his day at Uppsala, kept the talks going by personal correspondence after he left. In 1955 China released all fifteen detained airmen.
684.explanation: The mission succeeded through a combination of sound judgement, personal standing and deep learning, qualities the Nobel Committee and the UN later credited for what was called his first major victory.
684.tie_back: The kural asks for an envoy in whom good sense, an impressive presence and tested learning are combined, and Hammarskjold's Peking mission is an example of all three bringing a difficult task to success.
684._accuracy_note: Learning and judgement are well documented, but the sources say little specifically about his physical presence, so one of the three qualities is inferred rather than shown.

685.event_title: Ralph Bunche negotiates the 1949 armistice agreements on Rhodes
685.event: After the UN mediator Count Folke Bernadotte was killed in September 1948, his chief aide Ralph Bunche became acting mediator in the Arab-Israeli conflict. Working from the island of Rhodes through eleven months of almost continuous negotiation, he obtained signatures on separate armistice agreements between Israel and the individual Arab states. Time magazine credited the first agreement largely to his ability, patience, tact and unflagging good humour, and in 1950 he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
685.explanation: Bunche kept bitterly opposed parties at the table by tact and humour rather than pressure, and the agreements he secured stood as the framework for nearly two decades.
685.tie_back: The kural praises the envoy who avoids harsh words and speaks so pleasantly that his hearers are won over, and Bunche's tact and good humour at Rhodes are a modern example.
685._accuracy_note: A good fit for pleasant, tactful negotiation; the kural's specific point about condensing many demands into a brief statement is not documented in these sources.

686.event_title: Adlai Stevenson confronts Valerian Zorin at the UN Security Council
686.place: UN Security Council, New York, United States
686.event: During the Cuban Missile Crisis, the United States ambassador to the UN, Adlai Stevenson, pressed the Soviet representative Valerian Zorin in an open session of the Security Council to say whether the Soviet Union had placed missiles in Cuba. When Zorin would not answer directly, Stevenson had large reconnaissance photographs of the missile sites displayed to the Council. The JFK Library notes that the normally courteous Stevenson confronted Zorin aggressively that day.
686.explanation: Stevenson chose the moment and the evidence so that his case reached not only the Soviet delegate but the whole Council and the watching world.
686.tie_back: The kural asks for an envoy who speaks so that his words sink in, who does not flinch under a hostile glare, and who knows what the moment requires, which is what Stevenson did in the Council chamber.
686._accuracy_note: Close to a dramatisation of the kural's unflinching, well-timed speech before a hostile counterpart.

687.event_title: John Adams presents his credentials to King George III
687.event: John Adams, the first United States minister to Britain, presented his credentials to King George III less than a week after arriving in London, following eight years of war between the two countries. The audience followed the formal ceremony of the royal court, and Adams delivered a short address he had rehearsed and committed to memory, assuring the King of his country's wish for friendly relations. He reported the exchange, including the King's reply, to John Jay the next day.
687.explanation: Adams treated a delicate first meeting between former enemies with careful attention to court protocol and prepared words, and the King answered in kind.
687.tie_back: The kural describes the best envoy as one who knows the proper protocol, chooses the right moment and place, and thinks his words through before speaking, as Adams did before George III.
687._accuracy_note: Protocol and a rehearsed speech are documented; the choice of time and place was largely set by the court, so that part of the kural is only partly shown.

688.event_title: American envoys refuse the bribe demanded in the XYZ Affair
688.event: President John Adams sent Charles Cotesworth Pinckney, John Marshall and Elbridge Gerry to France to restore relations and protect American shipping. Intermediaries for the French foreign minister Talleyrand told them that negotiations would require a large loan to France and a personal bribe for Talleyrand. The envoys refused, Pinckney and Marshall prepared to leave, and when their dispatches were published in 1798 with the French agents' names replaced by the letters X, Y and Z, the demand caused a public outcry.
688.explanation: The envoys would not let money bend their mission and reported exactly what had happened, even though it meant failing to reach an agreement.
688.tie_back: The kural asks of the envoy who carries his master's message a purity that bribes cannot touch, boldness and truthfulness, all of which the American commissioners showed in Paris.
688._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of incorruptible, truthful envoys; the kural's point about having supporters at the foreign court is not part of this story.

689.event_title: Busbecq holds firm through years of confinement at Suleiman's court
689.event: Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, envoy of the Habsburg ruler Ferdinand I to Sultan Suleiman, presented demands at his first audience that he described as full of dignity and independence, and the Sultan received them coldly. On his second mission he and his staff were confined to their lodgings and treated almost as prisoners, and when his colleagues were allowed to leave in 1557 he chose to stay, judging that his departure would signal the end of talks and make war more likely. In 1562 he concluded a truce acceptable to both sides and returned to Vienna.
689.explanation: Under years of pressure and confinement, Busbecq neither abandoned his post nor gave way on his master's position, and his patience finally produced peace terms.
689.tie_back: The kural says only an envoy firm enough never to let a word that lowers his king slip out under pressure is fit to carry his message, and Busbecq's steadiness in Constantinople fits that demand.
689._accuracy_note: Shows firmness under pressure on behalf of his ruler; the sources describe his steadfastness rather than any specific words he refused to say.

690.event_title: Zhang Qian completes his mission to the Yuezhi after years of captivity
690.event: The Han emperor Wudi sent Zhang Qian to seek an alliance with the Yuezhi against the Xiongnu. Zhang was captured by the Xiongnu and held for about ten years, but escaped and continued westward until he reached the Yuezhi in the region of Bactria, then was captured again on his return journey. He finally got back to the court after an absence of about thirteen years and gave the emperor a detailed report on the lands he had seen.
690.explanation: Although the alliance he sought was refused, Zhang Qian carried his mission through at great personal risk and his full report opened Han China's contacts with Central Asia.
690.tie_back: The kural praises the envoy who fulfils his king's charge to the end even at the risk of his life, and Zhang Qian persisted through two captivities to complete and report on his mission.
690._accuracy_note: Strong on loyalty and persistence through mortal danger; the kural's focus on delivering a message to a foreign king word for word is only partly matched, since his embassy failed to win the alliance.
